fields.Front: Why can PROFESSOR (M) Teaches (N) COURSE not be mapped with a Teaches column?
fields.Back: The tempting column holds 'CS3319, CS2210' for Laura - a cell with more than one value, which is not in FIRST NORMAL FORM. Putting professor IDs into COURSE fails the same way (CS2210 has three professors). Neither side is a 'one' side, so there is nowhere to put a single foreign key.

fields.Front: Give the TEACHES table for: Laura (11) and Doug (22) teach CS3319; Doug, Laura and Jamie (34) teach CS2210; Doug teaches CS1027; Irving (56) and Stuart (18) teach MA2222.
fields.Back:
(CS3319, 11), (CS3319, 22), (CS2210, 11), (CS2210, 22), (CS2210, 34), (CS1027, 22), (MA2222, 18), (MA2222, 56). Primary key (EmpID, CourseNumber); both columns are also foreign keys, to PROFESSOR and COURSE.
Primary key of TEACHES = (EmpID, CourseNumber); both columns are ALSO foreign keys, to PROFESSOR and to COURSE respectively.

fields.Front: How does the instructor verify that (CourseNumber, EmpID) is a valid key for TEACHES, and how is a professor who teaches nothing represented?
fields.Back: No pair such as (CS3319, 11) appears twice; CourseNumber alone repeats and EmpID alone repeats, but the COMBINATION makes each row unique. Michael, who teaches nothing, simply has NO ROWS in TEACHES - no nulls are needed.

fields.Front: Map MOVIE (M) Stars (N) ACTOR with relationship attribute Salary.
fields.Back:
Movie (MovieID, Title, Cost, ReleaseDate)
Actor (ActorID, FirstName, LastName, BirthDate)
Starring (MovieID (FK), ActorID (FK), Salary) with primary key (MovieID, ActorID).
Salary is what this actor was paid for this movie - it depends on the pair, so it lives in the new table, but it is not part of the key.

fields.Front: How is a ternary relationship mapped, and what correction does the instructor make about the slide?
fields.Back: Take the key from EACH of the three entities, put them in a NEW table as foreign keys; together they form the new primary key; include any extra attributes. Abstract example: rr (aid (FK), bid (FK), cid (FK), rattr), PK (aid, bid, cid). Week 1's example: SUPPLY (SName, PartNo, ProjName, Quantity). Her correction: the slide should really read 'many to many to many'. Most relationships are binary; ternary ones are 'not as common' but the rule is the same.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: STUDENT (M) --- takes (Grade) --- (N) COURSE. Write the schema and mark the keys.
fields.Back:
STUDENT (StudentNum, FirstName, LastName)
COURSE (CourseNum, CourseName)
TAKES (StudentNum (FK), CourseNum (FK), Grade) with primary key (StudentNum, CourseNum).
Grade is a relationship attribute - it depends on the pair - so it goes in TAKES but is not part of the key and is not a foreign key.

fields.Text: An M:N relationship maps to a {{c1::NEW table}} whose primary key is {{c1::the combination of both entities' keys}}; those two columns are {{c1::also foreign keys}}, and any attributes of the relationship go into the new table but are not part of the key.

A ternary relationship is mapped by putting {{c1::all three keys}} in a new table as foreign keys; together they form the {{c1::primary key}}, and any extra attributes are included - e.g. {{c1::SUPPLY(SName, PartNo, ProjName, Quantity)}}.

Textbook (Elmasri §9.1.1, step 5): an M:N relationship has {{c1::only one}} mapping option - the relationship relation - because a single foreign key column cannot hold {{c1::more than one value}}, so no participating relation can absorb it. The new table is also called a {{c1::lookup table}}.
